etymology_text:
From Ancient Greek ὑπάγω (hupágō, “bring under”) in its Hellenistic sense "go", through its imperfect tense ὑπῆγον (hupêgon) > mediaeval ὑπῆγα (hupêga) which was wrongly analysed as ὑ- + πῆγα (instead of ὑπ- +) and a formation of a new mediaeval present tense + -αίνω (-aínō), πηγαίνω (pēgaínō), in the familiar pattern of aorist - present like ἔμαθα (ématha) - μαθαίνω (mathaíno, “learn”). The form πάω (páo), with silenced [ɣ] for <γ> of mediaeval ὑπάγω.
Also see the imperative άμε! (áme!), parallel form of πήγαινε! (pígaine!) and the mediaeval types ὑπαγαίνω (hupagaínō), ἀπηγαίνω (apēgaínō).

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek κλέβω (klébō), from Ancient Greek κλέπτω (kléptō, “steal”) from the aorist stem κλεψ- (kleps-) in the pattern of -ψ- > -β- as in κόπτω (kópto), κοψ- > κόβω (kóvo). The Ancient Greek derives from Proto-Hellenic *klépt͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *klép-ye-ti, from *klep-.
Cognate with Mariupol Greek клэ́фту (kléftu).

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek φράζω (phrázō) from Ancient Greek φράσσω (phrássō) or φράττω (phráttō) from past tense ‑αξα to present ‑άζω, in the pattern of στάζω (stázō), ἔσταξα (éstaxa, “I dripped”).
Unrelated to the ancient φράζω (phrázō, “tell, explain”). Stems φρακ-, φραγ- unrelated to φρακάρω (frakáro) or φράξια (fráxia) (see Related terms).

head_templates.name: el-verb
head_templates.expansion: ψάχνω • (psáchno) (past έψαξα, passive ψάχνομαι, p‑past ψάχτηκα, ppp ψαγμένος)

etymology_text: Inherited from Byzantine Greek ψάχνω (psákhnō), from Ancient Greek ψαύω (psaúō, “to touch (lightly)”), based on past tense stem's change ψαυσ- > ψαξ- and further metaplasm similar to the pattern διωξ-, έδιωξα (édioxa, past tense) - διώχνω (dióchno, “chase away”, present tense) - compare ancient διώκω (diṓkō). ψαύω (psaúō) is likely related to ψάω (psáō, “to touch lightly”); see there for more.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek ἀγναντεύω (agnanteúō), from the adverb ἀγνάντι (agnánti) or ἀγνάντια (agnántia, “vis-à-vis, opposite”) + -εύω (-eúō, “suffix for verbs”).
The also modern Greek αγνάντια (agnántia) derives from the Ancient Greek phrase τά ἐναντία (tá enantía, “what lies opposite”) through the medieval forms τα ἐνάντια (ta enántia) (with change of accent) > *ταϊνάντια (*taïnántia) (crasis of the two vowels α + ε) > ταγνάντια (tagnántia) ([ι > γ]). The adverbial form αγνάντι (agnánti) comes from the singular of the Ancient phrase *το ἐνάντι (*to enánti, “what lies opposite”).

glosses: to scan, survey (the horizon, look from afar)

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek χάνω (khánō), developed from ἔχασα (ékhasa), ἐχάσα (ekhása), from the Koine Greek aorist *ἐχάωσα (*ekháōsa) (infinitive χαῶσαι (khaôsai)) of a root *χαώνω (*khaṓnō), from the verb χαόω (khaóō), χαῶ (khaô), from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos). Cognate with Mariupol Greek хану (xanu).

examples.translation: She can't go anywhere without men relentlessly harassing her.
examples.english: She can't go anywhere without men relentlessly harassing her.

examples.english: The steak he ate didn't agree with him later on.

examples.english: Smoking harms health.

examples.text: Όχι, ευχαριστώ. Το ψάρι με πειράζει.

glosses: to affect (negatively), trouble, bother, not agree with (of food)

head_templates.expansion: φτιάχνω • (ftiáchno) active (past έφτιαξα, passive φτιάχνομαι, p‑past φτιάχτηκα, ppp φτιαγμένος)

etymology_text:
Ultimately from forms of Byzantine Greek εὐθειάζω (eutheiázō, “straighten, correct”) / εὐτειάζω, εὐθειάνω (eutheiánō) / εὐτειάνω, from Ancient Greek εὐθεῖα (eutheîa), feminine of εὐθύς (euthús, “straight”), + -άζω (-ázō). The exact morphological path is debated:
* Inherited from Byzantine Greek φτιάζω (phtiázō) as follows: past tense formation in the pattern of e.g. έπαιξα (épaixa), ancient ἔπαιξα (épaixa), stem παιξ- - present tense παίζω (paízo, “play”). Further formation of the new present tense φτιάχνω in the pattern of e.g. έριξα (érixa), ancient ἔρριξα (érrhixa, past tense), stem ριξ- - present tense ρίχνω (ríchno, “throw”). Compare to the colloquial φτιάνω (ftiáno) and the formation of vernacular varieties.
* Or, for the etymological spelling φτειάχνω (fteiáchno), a metaplasm of Byzantine Greek φτειάνω (phteiánō) / φθειάνω (phtheiánō) based on past stem of φτειάζω (phteiázō) / φτειάζω.

examples.text: Ο πρωθυπουργός δεν αποδέχθηκε την παραίτηση του υπουργού του.

etymology_text: Passive perfect participle of καλομαθαίνω (kalomathaíno, “to be spoiled”), an active-only verb. The stem μαθη- (mathi-) from the Ancient Greek μανθάνω (manthánō, “I learn”). From Byzantine Greek καλομαθαίνω (kalomathaínō): καλο- (“good, well”) + μαθαίνω (mathaíno, “to learn”).

examples.english: We have invited him to stay, treated him with care, but he is spoiled and nothing was to his liking.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Byzantine Greek ἀποσταίνω (apostaínō), through its passive aorist ἀποστάθηκα (apostáthēka) from stem αποστ- (apost-) of the ancient verb ἀφίσταμαι (aphístamai, “withdraw, stop”) and metaplasm to the verb suffix -αίνω (-aíno) in the pattern of verbs like ζεστάθηκα (zestáthika) ~ ζεσταίνω (zestaíno). Also see the Hellenistic form ἀφιστάνω (aphistánō).
A rare spelling αποστένω (aposténo), according to Andriotis, from the passive past ἀποστάθηκα (apostáthēka) of the Mediaeval form ἀποστέκω (apostékō).

etymology_text: κελαηδ(ώ) (kelaïd(ó)) + modern suffix -άω (-áo). Inherited from the medieval form Byzantine Greek κελαηδῶ (kelaēdô) (also spelling κελαϊδῶ (kelaïdô)) of κελαδῶ (keladô), from Ancient Greek κελαδῶ (keladô), contracted form of κελᾰδέω (kelădéō, “to sound as flowing water; to sing”), with diphthongisation of [a] > [ai̯]. etymology_text:
Inherited from Koine Greek δαγκάνω (dankánō) with metaplasm after -ώνω (-óno) verbs. From the root of δάκνω (dáknō), from Proto-Indo-European *denḱ-.
Or from Byzantine Greek δακώνω (dakṓnō), based on the ancient aorist ἔδακον (édakon), with the voicing of [k] influenced by Hellenistic Koine δαγκάνω.
Also see Etymology of δαγκάνω.

etymology_text: From the modern καταντ(ώ) (katant(ó)) + -άω (-áo). From the Hellenistic Koine Greek καταντῶ (katantô), contracted form of καταντάω (katantáo, “arrive at a point, come down to”), from κατά (katá) + ἀντῶ (antô, “I am opposite to”), uncontracted ἀντάω (antáō), from ἀντί (antí).

From κουτσο- (koutso-) (κουτσός (koutsós, “lame, limping”)) + an element μπολ- (bol-) + -εύω (-évo, “suffix for verbs”).
The element μπολ- (bol-) is most likely from the verb μπολιάζω (boliázo, “to graft onto, inoculate”), i.e. "to graft lame (speech)" > "to gossip". Alternatively, the element is from an earlier μπολεύω (bolévo, “I wander around”), from an unattested Hellenistic Koine Greek *ἐμπολεύω (*empoleúō, “to frequent, go about, trade”), from ἐν- (en-) + a contamination-driven blend of πολεύω (poleúō, “to wander, turn about”) and ἐμπολάω (empoláō, “to get by barter”).

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek γκρινιάζω (nkriniázō), γρινιάζω (griniázō). Either from γκρίνια (gkrínia, “moaning, complaining”) + -άζω (-ázo) (but possibly vice versa, a back-formation of γκρίνια from the verb). Or from dialectal Italian grignare (“grind teeth”) (contemporary Italian digrignare), from the Frankish *grīnan (“to grin”). Also, possible influence from the mediaeval synonym γρυνίζω (grunízō), associated to the ancient γρυλίζω (grulízō, “grunt”).

etymology_text: Formal, perfect tense participle in the fashion of the ancient participles, of the verb επαναλαμβάνομαι (epanalamvánomai, “I am repeated”), passive voice of modern επαναλαμβάνω or ancient ἐπαναλαμβάνω. Morphologically from επανα- (“again”) + ancient εἰλημμένος (eilēmménos, “who has been admitted”) or modern ειλημμένος (“who has been taken”). For spelling discussion see Etymology of ειλημμένος. Possibly, also a semantic loan of the English repeated.

examples.roman: Oi epaneilimménes mou ekklíseis den eisakoústikan.
examples.translation: My repeated appeals were not heard favourably.

etymology_text: Formal perfect participle of λαμβάνομαι (lamvánomai), passive voice of λαμβάνω (lamváno). In the fashion of the Hellenistic Koine Greek εἰλημμένος (eilēmménos, “who has been admitted”), participle of the ancient λαμβάνω (lambánō). The spelling with ει of its passive perfect tense εἴλημμαι (eílēmmai, “I have received”) comes from *σέ‑σληβ‑μαι. Τhe double μμ, from ληβ- + -μ- > λημμ-. Also, semantic loan from French pris.

etymology_text: βρομώ (vromó) + -άω (-áo). From Ancient Greek βρομῶ (bromô), contracted form of βρομέω (broméō, “to make loud noise”), from βρόμος (brómos, “loud noise”), from βρέμω (brémō, “to crash, to bang”). Related to βρόμη (vrómi, “oats”). Modern sense acquired from association of certain loud noises with a bad smell following. Compare Irish English bang (“strong smell”). See also Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink, stench”).

etymology_text: Perfect participle of πατιέμαι (patiémai), the passive voice of πατάω (patáo) (also πατώ (pató)).

examples.text: Υπάρχει ένα μονοπάτι […] ένα μονοπάτι πατημένο από αγόρια που κατεβαίνουν απ’ τ’ αγροκτήματα να κολυμπήσουν στη βαθιά λιμνούλα.
examples.ref: 2013, John Steinbeck, translated by Μιχάλης Μακρόπουλος, Άνθρωποι και ποντίκια, Εκδόσεις Παπαδόπουλος, →ISBN, page 10:
examples.english: There is a path […] a path trodden by boys coming down from the ranches to swim in the deep pool.
examples.roman: Ypárchei éna monopáti […] éna monopáti patiméno apó agória pou katevaínoun ap’ t’ agroktímata na kolympísoun sti vathiá limnoúla.
examples.translation: There is a path […] a path trodden by boys coming down from the ranches to swim in the deep pool.

examples.text: Σε κάποιο σημείο το χορτάρι είναι πατημένο, και φαίνεται σαν κάποιος να έχει περπατήσει στο έδαφος.
examples.ref: 2016, Caroline Eriksson, translated by Ξενοφών Παγκαλιάς, Οι εξαφανισμένοι, Ψυχογιός, →ISBN, page 18:
examples.english: At one point the grass is flattened, and it looks as if someone has walked on the ground.
examples.roman: Se kápoio simeío to chortári eínai patiméno, kai faínetai san kápoios na échei perpatísei sto édafos.
examples.translation: At one point the grass is flattened, and it looks as if someone has walked on the ground.

examples.text: […] με κρεβάτι κάτω απ’ την πλάτη μου το πατημένο χορτάρι […]
examples.ref: 2024, Benjamin Myers, translated by Ιωάννα Ηλιάδη, Η άκρη του ορίζοντα, Κλειδάριθμος, →ISBN, page 23:
examples.english: […] with the flattened grass as a bed beneath my back […]
examples.roman: […] me kreváti káto ap’ tin pláti mou to patiméno chortári […]
examples.translation: […] with the flattened grass as a bed beneath my back […]

raw_glosses: (of ground, a path, grass, etc.) trodden, flattened, or compacted
senses.qualifier: a path; grass; a path; grass

examples.text: […] πάτησε το κουμπί που του είχε υποδείξει και το κράτησε πατημένο.

examples.translation: […] he pressed the button he had been shown and kept it held down.

examples.text: Μέρα-μεσημέρι, μέσα στο Τμήμα, μετά από μια γεμιστά, μια χωριάτικη και μια μπυρίτσα, ο Αναστάσης υπερέβη τα όρια της συμπαγούς πραγματικότητας και μεταπήδησε στον άχρονο και άχωρο κόσμο του ονείρου.
examples.ref: 2011, Christidis Lenos, chapter 21, in Λοστρέ, page 311:
examples.english: In the middle of the day, inside the Department, after a gemista, a Greek salad and a beer, Anastasis transcended the limits of solid reality and jumped into the timeless and spaceless world of dreams.
examples.roman: Méra-mesiméri, mésa sto Tmíma, metá apó mia gemistá, mia choriátiki kai mia byrítsa, o Anastásis yperévi ta ória tis sympagoús pragmatikótitas kai metapídise ston áchrono kai áchoro kósmo tou oneírou.
examples.translation: In the middle of the day, inside the Department, after a gemista, a Greek salad and a beer, Anastasis transcended the limits of solid reality and jumped into the timeless and spaceless world of dreams.
